newsitem.title: USA: Croatia hopes to be NATO partner soon.
newsitem.headline: Croatia hopes to be NATO partner soon.

text.p: Croatia would like to join NATO's Partnership for Peace programme late this year or early 1998 and to be identified in 1999 as a possible NATO member, the Croatian ambassador to Washington said on Thursday.

"Our hopes are some time by the end of this year or maybe beginning of next year to become members of Partnership for Peace or to sign a Partnership for Peace contract," envoy Miomir Zuzul told reporters at a luncheon.

Partnership for Peace (PFP), which involves military cooperation programmes with NATO, includes most East European and former Soviet states and is seen by the Western alliance as a first stage for aspiring NATO members.
Croatia has not been able to join so far because of the ethnic conflicts that have afflicted it along with much of the rest of former Yugoslavia.

But Zagreb is hoping to put the conflicts behind it when it gains full control of the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, which has been under U.N. administration since last year. The last U.N. peacekeeping troops are due to leave in October and the last civilian administrators in January.
Zuzul said Croatia would like to be invited to apply for NATO membership in 1999, but realistically only hoped to be mentioned then as a potential member.

"If we have similar position like Slovenia and Romania now, and everybody knows that one day they will be eventually members of NATO, I think that that is realistically speaking also something that can satisfy our ideas," he said.

A NATO summit earlier this month invited Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to apply to join and picked out Romania and Croatia's neighbour, Slovenia, as promising contenders for the next round of NATO expansion.
U.S. officials have said, however, that there remain conditions for Croatia joining Western institutions including the Partnership For Peace, NATO and the European Union.
U.S. ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith said in May that these included Croatia permitting all Serb refugees and displaced persons to return to their former homes.

Zuzul said Zagreb also recognised that it stood no chance of joining NATO unless it cooperated with the Hague-based tribunal which has indicted suspects, some of them Croats, for war crimes in the Balkan conflict which raged from 1991-95.

He reaffirmed recent pledges by Croatian President Franjo Tudjman to assist the tribunal, but said Croatia could not send forces into Croat areas of neighbouring Bosnia to arrest war crimes suspects who have taken refuge there.
Zagreb says any indicted suspects found in Croatia will be sent to The Hague.
